questions.question: Why is String immutable in Java?
questions.title: String Immutability
questions.direct_answer: String is immutable because its internal char array is final and the class is final, giving thread safety, security, and caching benefits.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java fundamentals and design decisions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying 'you can't change a String' without explaining why or the benefits
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention security (HashMap keys, class loading) and String pool reuse

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: String is immutable by design — once created, its content never changes. The class is declared final so nobody can subclass it, and its internal character storage is never modified after construction. Every 'change' like concat or replace creates a brand new String object.

content: Thread safety: multiple threads can share the same String with zero synchronization
Security: class loaders, network connections, file paths use Strings — a mutable String could be changed after a security check passes
HashMap performance: hashCode is computed once and cached — immutability guarantees it never goes stale
String pool: identical literals can share one object safely because nobody can mutate it

beats.content: When you write s = s + "world", the original String is untouched. Java creates a new String and assigns the reference. That's why concat in a loop is expensive — N iterations create N objects.

sections.hook: Saying 'you can't change a String' misses the point. The real answer is why Java made that design choice — and there are three solid reasons.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So String immutability means once a String object is created, its value can never change. The way Java enforces this is: the String class is declared final so you can't subclass it, and internally it stores characters in a final char array — though what really matters is that no method ever modifies that array after construction.

The designers made this choice for three main reasons. First, thread safety — multiple threads can share the same String object with zero synchronization because nobody can change it. Second, security — class loaders use Strings for class names, network connections use Strings for hostnames. If Strings were mutable, malicious code could change the value after a security check passed. Third, caching — String is the most common HashMap key, and its hashCode can be computed once and cached because the value never changes.

Important: when you 'change' a String with concat or replace, Java creates a NEW String object. The original is untouched. That's why String concatenation in a loop is slow — you're creating N objects.

sections.title: Key Points
content: final class + final char[] field
Thread safe by design — no sync needed
hashCode cached (HashMap key performance)
Security: class names, network hosts can't be tampered
String + in loops creates N objects → use StringBuilder

questions.question: If String is immutable, why is String concatenation in a loop slow?
questions.title: String Concat Performance
questions.direct_answer: Each + creates a new String object, so concatenating N strings creates N intermediate objects and copies O(N²) characters total.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical awareness of String performance pitfalls
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying strings are slow without explaining the object creation cost
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that modern Java compiles simple concat to StringBuilder but NOT loops

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: Because Strings are immutable, + can't modify the existing string. It creates a brand new String object every iteration. A loop that builds a 1000-character string appending one character at a time creates 1000 objects and copies roughly 500,000 characters total — that's O(N squared) work.

content: StringBuilder maintains a resizable internal char array — append() just writes into it
StringBuilder creates one final String only when you call toString()
That reduces the work to O(N) — 1000 characters means 1000 writes, not 500,000 copies
Java compiler does optimize simple one-liner concat to StringBuilder — but cannot optimize a loop

beats.content: The compiler limit is important: each loop iteration is a separate expression. The compiler creates a new StringBuilder per iteration, not one shared instance across the loop. So the advice — use StringBuilder.append() in loops and call toString() once at the end — is still real and needed.

sections.hook: String + in a loop looks innocent but hides O(N squared) work. StringBuilder fixes it in one step.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So the problem with String concatenation in a loop is that every + operation creates a brand-new String object. Let's say you're building a 1000-character string by appending one character at a time. Iteration 1 creates a 1-char string, iteration 2 copies that 1 char plus the new char into a 2-char string, and so on. By the end you've created 1000 objects and copied roughly 500,000 characters total — that's O(N²) work.

StringBuilder solves this by maintaining a resizable char array internally. append() just writes into that array. You only create the final String once when you call toString(). That reduces it to O(N) work.

One thing to mention: the Java compiler does optimize simple String + calls into StringBuilder. But it cannot optimize a loop — each loop iteration produces a separate StringBuilder, converts it to String, and discards it. So 'use StringBuilder in loops' is still real advice.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Each + makes a new String object (immutability)
Loop concat = O(N²) copies
StringBuilder uses a resizable array → O(N)
Compiler optimizes one-liner concat but NOT loops
Use StringBuilder.append() in loops, toString() at the end

questions.question: How do you create an immutable class in Java?
questions.title: Creating Immutable Classes
questions.direct_answer: Make the class final, all fields private and final, initialize only in constructor, and never expose mutable object references directly.

interviewer_intent.testing: OOP design and defensive programming knowledge
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to deep-copy mutable fields like Lists or arrays in the constructor and getter
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the defensive copy pattern for mutable fields

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: The recipe for an immutable class has five steps. Get all five right and nothing outside can change the object's state.

content: Declare the class final — prevents subclasses from adding mutation
Make all fields private and final — no direct access, no reassignment
Initialize all fields only in the constructor — no setters
Defensive copy for mutable inputs: if a List is passed in, store new ArrayList<>(list) not the original reference
Defensive copy in getters: return new ArrayList<>(this.list) not this.list

beats.content: The defensive copy step is where most candidates slip up. If you store the exact List reference the caller passed, they can mutate it later and change your supposedly immutable object. Java records (Java 16+) automate the boilerplate for simple data holders — but you still own the defensive copy logic.

sections.hook: Most candidates say 'final fields and no setters'. That's incomplete. The real trap is mutable fields that still leak mutation even after you declare them final.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So the recipe for an immutable class has five steps. First, declare the class as final so nobody can subclass it and override methods to add mutation. Second, make all fields private and final. Third, set all fields only in the constructor — no setters. Fourth, if any field is a mutable object like a List or array, make a defensive copy in the constructor so external code can't change it after passing it in. Fifth, if you provide a getter for a mutable field, return a copy of it, not the reference.

The classic trap is forgetting the defensive copy. Say you have an immutable class with a List field. If you store the exact reference passed in, the caller can still modify the list externally and change your 'immutable' object's state. So you do `this.list = new ArrayList<>(list)` in the constructor and `return new ArrayList<>(this.list)` in the getter.

String itself is immutable following these principles. Java record classes (Java 16+) give you immutability automatically for simple data holders.

sections.title: Key Points
content: final class
private final fields
Constructor-only initialization, no setters
Defensive copy for mutable fields (List, array) in constructor
Defensive copy in getter
Java records auto-immutable for simple cases

questions.question: How does String's immutability enable hashCode caching?
questions.title: hashCode Caching
questions.direct_answer: String computes hashCode once and caches it in a private field — immutability guarantees the value never changes, so the cached hashCode is always valid.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not connecting immutability to HashMap performance
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain cached hashCode makes String the ideal HashMap key

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: String has a private int hash field initialized to zero. The first time you call hashCode(), it computes the value from all the characters and stores it in that field. Every subsequent call just returns the cached value — O(1) instead of O(n).

content: Mutable objects cannot safely cache hashCode — changing the content would invalidate the cache
Immutability guarantees the characters never change, so the cached hash is always correct
This is a major reason String is the ideal HashMap and HashSet key
Every HashMap.get(key) call triggers hashCode() — cached means no recomputation

sections.hook: String is the most popular HashMap key in Java. One reason: its hashCode is computed once and never recalculated. Immutability makes that safe.

sections.title: Key Points
content: String has private int hash field (0 = uncached)
First hashCode() computes from chars, stores in hash field
Subsequent calls return cached value — O(1)
Mutable objects cannot safely cache hashCode
This is why String is the most common HashMap key

questions.question: Why is the String class declared final in Java?
questions.title: Why String is Final
questions.direct_answer: String is final to prevent subclasses from breaking immutability guarantees — a mutable subclass could compromise security, caching, and thread safety.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking final just prevents inheritance without knowing the security motivation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the attack scenario: subclass overriding charAt() to return different values post-security-check

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: If String were not final, you could subclass it and override methods like charAt() to return different characters each time they're called. That breaks the immutability contract completely.

content: Attack scenario: pass a MutableString subclass to a security check — it shows safe content; after the check passes, charAt() returns something different
Class loaders use String for class names — a mutable class name could load a different class than checked
The final keyword ensures every String instance behaves identically to what the JDK specifies
All Java wrapper classes — Integer, Double, Boolean — are also final for the same reason

beats.content: Immutability without final is incomplete. The fields being final only prevents reassignment inside the class. A subclass could still introduce new mutable fields and override methods. Final closes that loophole.

sections.hook: Most people say 'final prevents subclassing'. The deeper answer: without final, a subclass could silently break every security guarantee Java builds on top of String.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Without final: attacker subclasses String, overrides methods
Security checks on String (class names, file paths) could be bypassed
All wrapper classes (Integer, Double, etc.) are also final for same reason
final ensures every String instance behaves identically
Immutability guarantee only works if class cannot be extended
